name: Pedro Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior in the office at a primary school, about three hundred children, on the edge of a small town. I do the morning register calls to parents when a child's missing, the letters home, the trip bookings, the dinner money and the cover rota when a teacher's off sick. Mrs Okafor, the office manager, does the budget and the harder stuff. I'm still learning the system for the registers, which crashes every other Monday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the children, and that the work has a rhythm: register, dinner money, letters, home time. What wears me out is parents who shout at the office because the trip's full. My wife Lucia helps at her parents' bakery, and we're trying to save for a deposit, but we've got maybe three weeks of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a few handy tricks, nothing that changes how a school runs. At church I'd say the same if anyone asked. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job's fine. Schools change slowly, and parents want a person on the phone. The pay's still poor, though, and a school office job doesn't move up quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd ask Mrs Okafor to teach me the budget side so I can step up when she retires. I'd use the AI for the newsletter, since the head's fine with it. And Lucia and I would keep putting fifty pounds a month toward the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A bit stuck on money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI at the school now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. The head said we could use it for the newsletter, and it saves me an hour on a Friday. I always check it, because it once invited parents to a sports day on a Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're saving for a deposit with three weeks put by. How's that going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. At fifty pounds a month, my wife and I will have a house deposit by the time we're fifty. We laugh about it, but it's not that funny.

say: I'd say it's a few **handy tricks**, nothing that changes a school.
I'd say the same at **church** if anyone asked.
think: Privately my job's **fine**, since parents want a person on the phone.
The **poor pay** and slow promotion are what bother me.
do: Ask Mrs Okafor to teach me the **budget side**.
Keep saving **fifty pounds** a month toward the deposit.
feel: **Settled**, but a bit stuck on money.
S0.quote: At fifty pounds a month, my wife and I will have a house deposit by the time we're fifty.
fieldNote: Pedro sees the school as **slow to change**, which steadies him.
His real frustration is a **house deposit** that feels out of reach.
He uses AI **lightly and carefully**, after the Sunday sports day mistake.

steps.text: Learn the school budget from Mrs Okafor before she retires
Use AI to draft the Friday newsletter
Keep saving fifty pounds a month for the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools are about people, so they'll keep people in the office. I'd probably believe it, too, at least out loud. At church I'd say we should look after the young ones coming into work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, letters, trip bookings and the cover rota are exactly the kind of thing a program does. The register calls might stay. But the council would see two people in a school office and ask why not one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new system as soon as it arrived, because I'd want to be the one who knows it. I'd look at the electrician apprenticeship at the college, the adult one, which my uncle did at thirty. And we'd stop the deposit savings for a while to keep a bigger cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like the school and I'd hate to lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bits of your day would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The letters and the bookings, then the rota. A computer could plan the teacher cover rota in a minute, and that takes me most of Monday morning. What's left is the phone and the first aid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucia say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia would say trust God and learn a trade. Her dad would say the same, louder. They'd both mean it kindly.

say: I'd say schools are about **people** and will keep staff in the office.
At church I'd say we should look after **young workers**.
think: Privately **letters, bookings and rotas** are exactly what a program does.
The council would see **two office staff** and ask why not one.
do: Learn the **new system** as soon as it arrives.
Look at the adult **electrician apprenticeship** at the college.
Pause deposit saving to keep a **bigger cushion**.
feel: **Anxious**, because he'd hate to lose the school.
S1.quote: A computer could plan the teacher cover rota in a minute, and that takes me most of Monday morning.
fieldNote: Pedro's public line is about **people**, but privately he expects cuts.
He considers a **trade**, following an uncle who retrained at thirty.
His wife's family offers **faith and practical** advice.

steps.text: Learn the school's new admin system as soon as it arrives
Ask the college about the adult electrician apprenticeship
Pause the deposit fund to keep cash on hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when families and churches have to hold each other up. I'd say people need work, not just a payment from the government. At the school I'd try to stay calm for the children's sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the school office is gone by 2028. Maybe one person stays for the phone, and it would be Mrs Okafor. I'd be out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician apprenticeship straight away, even on apprentice pay. I'd ask Lucia's dad for Saturday work in the bakery. And we'd move in with her parents to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like the ground's moving under the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that change your thinking about the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a lot. An electrician wiring a house in 2030 still has a job, and a school office junior doesn't. Three years is enough to qualify, just about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit becomes the money we live on. That's the hardest part to say.

say: I'd say **families and churches** must hold each other up.
I'd say people need **work**, not just a government payment.
think: Privately I think the **school office** is gone by 2028, apart from one phone.
If one person stays, it's **Mrs Okafor**, not me.
do: Ask Lucia's dad for **Saturday work** at the bakery.
Move in with **Lucia's parents** to save rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the ground's moving under the school.
S2.quote: An electrician wiring a house in 2030 still has a job, and a school office junior doesn't.
fieldNote: Pedro uses the **robot delay** to justify a trade, timing it to qualify.
He'd spend the **deposit** to live, which pains him.

steps.text: Start the adult electrician apprenticeship straight away
Work Saturdays at Lucia's family bakery
Move in with Lucia's parents to stop paying rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and people should learn a trade while they can. At the school I'd tell the other juniors. I'd say it plainly at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to qualify properly and keep the school job part of the time. That feels much better. My job still goes, but I'd land somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start the apprenticeship part-time and keep the school job in the mornings. I'd keep the deposit savings going, smaller. By 2030 I'd want to be a qualified electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. It's hard work, not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would you still go for the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd rather be an electrician in 2031 than the last person in a school office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lucia still try for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd wait a couple of years. I'd want to be a qualified electrician before Lucia (my wife) and I have our first baby.

say: I'd say five years is **fair warning** to learn a trade.
I'd say it plainly at **church** and to other juniors.
think: Privately I'd have time to **qualify properly** while keeping some school hours.
My job **still goes**, but I'd land somewhere.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** part-time in year one.
Keep the **school job** in the mornings.
feel: **Anxious but hopeful**, hard work rather than hopeless.
S3.quote: I'd want to be a qualified electrician before Lucia (my wife) and I have our first baby.
fieldNote: Five years lets Pedro **blend** school work with an apprenticeship.
His view of work as **dignity** shapes every choice.

steps.text: Keep the school mornings while training
Wait two years before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and people should use it wisely, not panic. I'd say a trade is a good thing to have whatever happens. At work I'd keep my head down and do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is enough to be qualified and working before the end point. Robots don't do wiring until about 2039. That's a long working life away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the school a couple more years, learn the budget side, save. Then I'd do the apprenticeship from about 2029. Lucia and I would buy a small house if we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not much. More like planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there less hurry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less hurry, but I don't trust myself to keep waiting. So I'd set a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the school children, if they asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to be good at something with their hands and something with people. A child who can fix a light and comfort a friend will always find work. That's what my grandmother told me, roughly.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so use it wisely.
I'd say a **trade** is good to have whatever happens.
think: Privately ten years is enough to be **qualified and working** before the end point.
do: Stay at the school **two more years** and save.
Buy a **small house** if we can.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, more like planning than worrying.
S4.quote: A child who can fix a light and comfort a friend will always find work.
fieldNote: With ten years, Pedro sees a **full career** in a trade.
He sets a **date** because he doesn't trust himself to wait.
His grandmother's advice on **hands and people** guides him.

steps.text: Stay at the school two more years and save
Buy a small house with Lucia if savings allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is just about enough to start a trade, but not to finish one. What would help is apprenticeships that pay enough to live on, for people my age, not just school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the children. The children in our school will grow up never having rung an office to say they're poorly, and I don't know what that does to them.

headlineQuote: The children in our school will grow up never having rung an office to say they're poorly, and I don't know what that does to them.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** junior in a primary school office.
He's married to Lucia and saving slowly for a **house deposit**.
He uses AI **now and then**, mainly for the newsletter.
Faith and **family** shape his choices more than government.
He's uneasy in calmer pictures, **alarmed** under AGI by 2028, and plans an electrician apprenticeship.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with time to start a trade but not finish it.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults, not only school leavers.
